description: THE ONE DECLARATION of which strings must be scrubbed out of a log before
it leaves a customer's cluster.
Before this file the rule existed as three hand-maintained copies and
nothing derived from anything: controller.py's _LOG_REDACTIONS, the OTTL
replace_pattern calls in the client chart's telemetry-collector ConfigMap,
and a chart test holding hand-written fragments of the second. They agreed
only because one person changed them in one sitting. The proof that this
matters: for as long as all three existed the generic pattern anchored its
keyword with \b on both sides, so every environment-variable spelling of a
secret -- AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET=, MYSQL_PASSWORD=, DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=,
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY= -- fell straight through, in every copy, with
passing tests on both sides (backend#1908, client#799, client-runtime#372).
Both consumers now DERIVE from this file:
* controller.py compiles `redactions` into _LOG_REDACTIONS at import.
* the client chart vendors this file into the chart and GENERATES the
OTTL statements from it, so no hand port of a regex exists anywhere.
client is a separate repository and GITHUB_TOKEN is repo-scoped, so the
chart cannot read this file at CI time without a credential. It vendors a
byte-identical copy plus the digest in .log-redactions.sha256 and checks
the two locally, with no network. THE HONEST COST: adopting a change here
is a TWO-PR ritual -- land it in this repo (bumping the digest), then land
the vendored copy, the digest and the pin in tracebloc/client. The digest
test below is what makes step two impossible to forget silently.
replacement_syntax: RE2 / Go: a capture group is `$1`, which is what OpenTelemetry's OTTL
replace_pattern consumes verbatim. controller.py converts `$N` to `\N`
for python's re.sub -- one mechanical conversion in one function, tested,
rather than a human retyping a regex. `${...}` named-group syntax is
REFUSED by that converter rather than mistranslated.
pattern_syntax: The intersection of python `re` and Go RE2 that both engines read the same
way: inline (?i)/(?im) flags, \b, character classes, bounded repeats. No
lookaround and no backreferences INSIDE a pattern -- RE2 has neither, and
an invalid regex in OTTL is a processor that starts and scrubs nothing.
Over-redaction is acceptable here; losing the diagnosis is not, which is
why the chart guard replays diagnosis specimens as well as secret ones.

redactions.why: scheme://user:pass@host -- corporate-proxy credentials, DB and broker URLs.
Azure / ServiceBus / Storage keys inside connection strings. The trailing Name= form (SharedAccessKeyName) is not a secret and is deliberately left intact for diagnosis.
Authorization / x-api-key headers -- the whole value, to end of line.
Bearer / DRF Token credentials wherever they appear.

why: THE NAME MAY CARRY A PREFIX, which is what the leading [\w.-]* is for.
The earlier form anchored the keyword with \b on each side, so it caught
a bare password= and missed every environment-variable spelling, because
_ is a word character and there is therefore no boundary between the
prefix and the keyword. Those are the shapes this stack actually prints:
backend#2069 deliberately names which AZURE_* variable is unset when
A FREE TRAILING [\w.-]* WAS TRIED AND IS WRONG: it made
SharedAccessKeyName= match -- prefix Shared, keyword AccessKey, suffix
Name -- and redact a key NAME that is not a secret. So the compound
endings live in the alternation instead (secret[_-]?key before secret,
alternation being leftmost-first) and there is no free suffix.
The optional opening quote matters for a related reason: without it
SECRET_KEY='x9y8z7' fell out entirely, because the value class excludes
quotes and so matched nothing after the separator.
